quotes.text: The album marks a new, more adventurous chapter in his career by investing in emotionally rich storytelling and stylistic exploration that shifts from blues to acoustic ballads and swaggering hard rock like nothing to it.

Bonamassa is not one of those artists that I would expect to blow things up in an indiscriminate manner, but rather season the blues template with whatever spices sprinkled in moderation, and what he adds to the age-old blues paradigm is pretty damn succulent.
Joe Bonamassa is no doubt a musician worthy of a place in the Mount Rushmore of great blues titans, and his new album speaks with the accent of true blues authority and certitude.

Cast aside all preconceived ideas you may have as Breakthrough sees Joe herald a fresh approach. The horns and orchestration of recent albums are nowhere to be found as Joe delights with ten brand new original songs, each one delivering a story with soulful heartfelt vocals encased in a rocky outer shell.
Joe reminds us he's a blues guitarist at heart during I'll Take The Blame.
Demonstrating a fresh approach to his sound this song has a groovy air of danceability to it enhanced by handclaps, a gang vocal and plentiful tinkling of the ivories.

With over 50 albums to choose from it would be inappropriate and unfair to proclaim this as Joe's best ever album but Breakthrough is certainly up there as one of his best, demonstrating the constant evolution of his sound. Joe's vocals, storytelling and songwriting walking hand in hand with his six string skills to make this album the success story it is destined to be.

'Breakthrough' also boasts the shorter, tighter, songwriting Bonamassa abandoned for the more widescreen, epic, some may say artsy, Pink Floyd-inflected approach he favored on 'Time Clocks.' While that showed the guitarist's penchant to explore other genres and expand his palette, longtime followers will likely rejoice in his nod to a more direct attack.
Like most of Bonamassa's recordings, he smartly alters the groove.
Perhaps the noticeable lack of extended guitar solos—they pepper each tune, but are never overdone–addresses that.
The outro guitar solo from JB's Les Paul is a heart-rending ride through the emotional hell of grief: denial, anger, bargaining, acceptance and, finally, resignation to the abyss of their anguish.
And "Mountain Time" is a total re-imagining of how it sounded when it was released, on the 2002 album "So It's Like That." JB said he'd never felt comfortable with it, so he kept retooling it.
in it, he proves that, despite his long career (he's 39 now), he's still a powerful and innovative presence in blues.
